title: A 9B with an agentic search loop beat a 35B MoE with one-shot retrieval
content:
A 9B with an agentic search loop beat a 35B MoE with one-shot retrieval
The software around the model mattered more than its size: a dense 9B with agentic search beat a 35B MoE with one-shot retrieval. Second finding: a 3B-active MoE kept up with a dense 27B.
Everyone compares models. For questions on your own documents, my gut tells me the software around the model matters at least as much. The engine may be strong, but what reaches the road also depends on the gearbox. So how much of an agent’s performance comes from the model, and how much from the software around it? I sat down and measured my gut feeling.
I asked questions about 14 official reports. The reports are newer than the models; none of the models could know them. I let each model answer in two ways. In one-shot retrieval (one search up front), the app searches once and hands the model the hits. In the other mode, the model searches itself, in a loop: it writes a search query, reads the hits, searches specifically for what is still missing, and only answers once it has enough. This is called agentic search. A second question came along: same size, mixture-of-experts (MoE) vs dense, what would you still pick the dense model for today? In many company RAG setups I come across (RAG: questions answered from retrieved document passages), a dense model of around 30B still does the work, one that uses all its parameters for every token.
Short version. Without search, no model found more than 5 of 233 facts (2 %). The software mattered most, not the model. One model, the MoE Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, uses about 3B of its 35B parameters per token. With one-shot retrieval it found 48 % of the facts; with agentic search it found 77 %. A dense 9B with agentic search found 65 % (one run) and beat the MoE with one-shot retrieval. With one-shot retrieval, the 4B, 9B and MoE were only 11 points apart. My second finding follows from that: with good search software, a MoE with 3B active parameters is enough. With agentic search, the MoE is level with the dense Qwen3.6-27B, a model of similar size (27B against 35B) that also used agentic search: 77 % against 78 %. The MoE is about 3 times as fast. Three attempts to favour the dense model, plus a check with the 9B, left the two level.
In one sentence: before you put money into a bigger model or more GPUs, look at the software around it; and if your machine can hold the MoE, there is little reason to pick a dense model for RAG. Two conditions: the MoE needs about 13 GB of memory plus the context, and I only measured one model family, Qwen3.6.
What I measured, and what not
Disclosure: I build Matrix, the app I measured in. I did not ask which model is cleverer. In my experience, people mostly use models of this size locally for RAG. Many organisations cannot send their documents to a cloud model.
I measured in Matrix, my app for asking questions about your own documents. Matrix offers both modes, one-shot retrieval and agentic search. The app does the fixed part (splitting, hybrid search, checking every quote against its source) and keeps a full trace of every answer. Matrix runs on macOS, iOS and Windows. The obvious objection is that it all comes down to my app. But both modes ran in the same app. So the finding is agentic search against one-shot retrieval, not my app against others; it can be rebuilt with any agent framework, and appendix A describes agentic search step by step.
The main set is 14 official reports from audit offices and accident investigation boards, in German and English. For the cross-check I used the Rogers Commission report on the Challenger accident, which is surely in every training set. MoE and 27B both ran as UD-IQ3_XXS (roughly 3 bits per weight) on llama.cpp, GPU only, thinking off. I scored every answer automatically; then model agents checked every answer again in a blind second review.
1. Knowledge does not help
On the unknown reports no model gets more than about 2 % without search, while on Challenger the frontier model already knows 47 % from memory.
Example. Under Horizon 2020’s InnovFin instruments, what share of recipients were SMEs, what share of the financing did they get, and which design feature excluded many smaller firms? Correct answer: 47 % of recipients, only 14 % of financing (€1.42 billion of €10.5 billion); minimum loan thresholds, often €25 million. Without search, MoE: “90–95 % of recipients; 40–50 % of financing, €15–17 billion” · Claude Opus 5.5: “cannot give exact figures” With agentic search, MoE: every figure of the correct answer, e.g. “47 % of recipients, 14 % of financing”.
Everything below refers to the unknown reports. Where I give Challenger numbers, I say so; Challenger without search is in appendix B.1.
2. The software around the model is the biggest lever
Agentic search adds 29 points for the MoE over one-shot retrieval, more than the gap between any two models that search the same way.
One-shot retrieval is the classic setup: hybrid search, a reranker (a second model that re-sorts the hits by relevance), the top 5 passages, one answer. With one-shot retrieval the MoE found 48 %, the 9B 40 % and the 4B 37 %. With the same software, a 4B and a 35B were 11 points apart. With agentic search, even the dense 9B found 65 % (one run). On Challenger the 9B with agentic search found 68 %, the MoE with one-shot retrieval 45 %. On Challenger the MoE itself rose from 45 % with one-shot retrieval to 86 % with agentic search.
Example. How high were the commitment credit for the programme renewal ZEMIS and its two tranches, by how much and when did the Federal Council cut the funds, and how high are the reserves against one project’s extra need? Correct answer: CHF 50.66 million; second tranche 28.66 million, first 22.00 million; cut of CHF 17.9 million on 28 January 2026; reserves 15.5 million against an extra need of 6.2 million. MoE, one-shot retrieval: “The documents do not give the credit, tranches, date or reserves; they only mention a cut of 17.9 million.” MoE, agentic search: every figure of the correct answer, e.g. “cut 17.9 million on 28 January 2026; reserves 15.5 against 6.2 extra need”.
Small settings count too. A single default of the app, the number of hits per search, decided whether the 27B got all passages it needed for 77 % or for 89 % of the facts (seed 1337, section 4). The score did not show that. I only saw it in the trace Matrix keeps for every answer: over both seeds the 27B left the number at the default of 6 in 110 of 154 search calls, while the MoE asked for 10 in 115 of 147. Without the trace I would have compared search and reading as one number.
3. With good software, a 3B-active MoE is enough
Both models used agentic search. The MoE (35B) found 77 % and the dense 27B, a model of similar size, 78 %; the MoE needed 22 seconds per question against 65.
On the 12 questions where neither model got full marks in any seed, the MoE found 47 % and the 27B 50 %. On Challenger they found 447 and 446 of 522 facts. An old rule of thumb from r/LocalLLaMA (2024) puts a MoE near a dense model with √(total × active) parameters, about 10B here. Qwen’s model card puts the 35B-A3B close to their older dense Qwen3.5-27B on coding and agent benchmarks. A MoE at the level of the 27B does not behave like a 10B. The real difference is speed. The MoE reads the prompt about three times as fast and writes 131 against 44 tokens per second. Agentic search rereads a growing prompt in every round, so that speed adds up.
Dense models are far from gone. On Hugging Face, the most downloaded of the 20–40B models right now is a dense 27B (Qwen3.8; Hugging Face, last 30 days, 9 November 2026). For RAG on your own documents, I would still test the MoE with good search software first.
4. Three attempts to give the dense model a better chance, and one check
Three times I tried to give the dense model a better chance; in total the two stay level, apart from a slight reading edge for the dense model.

report.summary: A dense 9B model running an agentic search loop beat a 35B MoE using one-shot retrieval on document QA, showing retrieval software outweighs raw model size.
report.background: Most local RAG setups — asking questions over your own documents — still follow the classic pattern: hybrid search once, rerank the hits, feed the top passages to the model, get an answer. Model choice dominates the discussion, but a growing camp argues the orchestration around the model matters just as much. Meanwhile the dense-vs-mixture-of-experts debate has sharpened: MoE models activate only a fraction of parameters per token, promising big-model quality at small-model speed, while dense models remain the default in most enterprise RAG stacks around 30B. The author, who builds the document-QA app Matrix, tested both assumptions on 14 official audit and accident-investigation reports published after the models' training cutoffs, so no model could rely on memorized knowledge, running everything locally via llama.cpp.
key_points: Without search, no model scored above about 2% of 233 facts on the unseen reports. The same frontier model already knew 47% of facts from memory on the Challenger report, which sits in every training set. Memorization, not reasoning, explains most apparent 'knowledge' gains.

Agentic search — the model writes queries, reads hits, and searches again for gaps — added 29 points for the 35B MoE, lifting it from 48% to 77%. That gain is larger than the gap between any two models searching the same way, making retrieval strategy the single biggest lever measured.

Retrieval mode beat parameter count outright: a dense 9B with agentic search reached 65% and beat the 35B MoE's one-shot 48%. In one-shot mode, 4B, 9B and 35B models were only 11 points apart, suggesting model size does little if the search loop is weak.

With agentic search on both sides, a MoE activating 3B of 35B parameters matched a dense 27B (77% vs 78%) while running roughly three times faster — 22 vs 65 seconds per question — because agentic loops reread a growing prompt every round, so token throughput compounds.

Small settings matter as much as architecture: the app's default hits-per-search decided whether the 27B got 77% or 89% of facts. Only per-answer traces revealed the 27B stuck at 6 hits in 110 of 154 calls while the MoE asked for 10.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the result reframes the scaling conversation: orchestration and retrieval loops can substitute for parameters, at least in document QA, so budget spent on bigger models or more GPUs may be better spent on search software. For developers, it argues for shipping agentic loops, exposing per-answer traces, and tuning retrieval knobs rather than chasing benchmark rankings; MoE models become the sensible default for local RAG when memory allows (~13GB plus context). For regular users, the practical effect is faster, cheaper local answers over private documents that never leave the machine — with the caveat that it is one model family (Qwen3.6) and one app's implementation.
report.tools: Try llama.cpp for local inference of GGUF-quantized Qwen3.6 dense and MoE models, and watch implementations of agentic RAG loops in LangGraph or LlamaIndex, plus hybrid search with a reranker (BM25 plus a bge or Cohere-style reranker). Matrix, the author's app, exposes both retrieval modes and per-answer traces for reproducing the comparison; any agent framework can rebuild the loop, and the article's appendix documents it step by step.
